Make 100-120 calls a day to hopefully pitch and close but when the client hears â€œYelpâ€ CLICK hang up!

Every day brought the opportunity to partner with local businesses, understand their goals, and guide them on how to use Yelp’s advertising tools to grow their visibility and attract new customers. I loved being able to combine data, strategy, and genuine human connection to help business owners feel more confident in their marketing decisions.

The role pushed me to stay organized, think quickly, and provide clear, patient support even in challenging moments. It taught me how to manage a full book of business, exceed performance targets, and communicate complex ideas in simple, helpful ways. Working with such a diverse group of clients also strengthened my ability to adapt my tone and approach to meet each person’s needs.

Overall, my time at Yelp gave me a deep appreciation for customer success work and confirmed how much I enjoy helping people achieve meaningful results. It was a positive, growth-focused environment that shaped me into a stronger, more effective professional.

review_title: Nothing in Sales is a Guarantee
review_text:
What is the best part of working at the company?
I’d have to say meeting new people and learning about different industries were the best part of working at this company. 

Also the benefits were pretty decent. 

What is the most stressful part about working at the company?
The most stressful part of working for YELP would have to be the toll it takes on your Mental Health. Managers stress you because their Job security is based off of how you perform. Also, the product doesn’t work for all industries but you are required to sell by any means even when you know it’s only going to waste the business owners Money. The worst part has to be when business owners call you back crying that’s they’ve received no return and may have to close the business, but there’s nothing you can do except prepare to sell the same product to the next client. It’s an atmosphere that feels like you’re hired to harass people 80% of the time. 
Another major stress would have to be pay structure. Working in sales nothing is promised because people do cancel. In this Economy people are securing their money but its stressful for you to get commission and if a client doesn’t stay on the platform you are now in a deficit, it’s like constantly playing catch up or getting a loan from the company with wavering terms. 

What is the work environment and culture like at the company?
The work environment is decent because of the events both virtual and local that you get access to, Alongside the different incentives they use to entice you to overlook that the product you’re selling is a hit or miss. Depending on the Manager your work environment can be encouraging or overwhelming.

review_title: Good for a first time sales position
review_text: Good for a first time sales job, or to transition to remote work. There is a constant false sense of urgency. Managers demand AE's make 80+ dials to angry business owners every day hard selling them to start using Yelp ads. Most of them have tried Yelp before and lost money, so you get very angry business owners. I have been verbally abused daily. Every day coming to work is a nightmare, but the flexibility to work remotely because of childcare keeps me here, until I find something else. The pay is terrible compared to other Senior Account Executive roles, and my sales team is often told to make a sale or leave. My manager even tells us she will help us find a new job.  Its a horribly toxic environment. Very few people ever leave the outbound sales role. To move out of your current role you have to hit target of your KPI's for 3 months plus and then often you're told, not this cycle but do it again and maybe will talk about your options. Considering the toxic work culture, high volume of calls required, and all of the stress the PTO policy isn't enough time.  The Yelp plan is to use up every drop of energy you have until you burn out and then the harrass you with daily threats about firing you until most people buckle to the pressure and quit.

review_title: The most supportive and best atmosphere ever - so much fun - you will be shocked that work can be this great
review_text:
What is the best part of working at the company?
The people - oh, my gosh - the best people to work for and with

What is the most stressful part about working at the company?
Making the requisite number of calls per day and making quota

What is the work environment and culture like at the company?
So supportive and a lot of fun

What is a typical day like for you at the company?
Lots of interaction with my team and manager, plus talking to potential clients

I clock in at 7am, manager passive aggressively throws shade at part of the team, the whole team, or just a select 1-2 people. Have to report when we start dialing, then have to make at least 85 dials, pitch twice, close once, and have at least 2 hours of talk time all in under 6 hours. So many meetings and redundant trainings for even the most successful reps who should be getting phone time instead. They can take your commission depending on retention, which many people cancel.

It's a great company if you are super tenacious and aren't bothered by micro management, redundant work, and a lot of rejection. The benefits are generous and the commission is uncapped. They have nice bonuses and you basically control how much money you make. Once in a while you actually get to help a business owner too, so that's really rewarding. It's not a bad job - it's just really hard!

review_title: No job security, Micromanagement, Amazing co-workers
review_text:

I learned a lot about small businesses and how digital marketing can impact their business goals.

Management is the reason I resigned from this job.  Upper management (Director)
puts so much pressure on the sales managers that directly affected the sales team.  

This statement is hearsay but 75% of sales reps hate their job and dread coming into work.  Yes, this is a performance-based job, but management is selective on what territories they give to their "favorite reps" meaning they get the highest yielding territory as well as additional "bonus" territories.   

The hardest part of the job was staying positive throughout the day.   You talk to a lot of unsatisfied customers that are rude and tired of Yelp.  The biggest part of the job was over coming objections, with past advertisers.  Yelp's favorite line to sales reps "get comfortable being uncomfortable" but every day is a bit much on your mental state.

The best part of the job is that I met some amazing people.  Great team environment.  Team members are very supportive of one another making the job fun.  Yelp hires some very talented people that don't get a fair chance to thrive and end up quitting or getting fired.  I saw at least 20+ people get fired in one year.  They fired people so frequently that you figured out the signs and knew it was coming.  Again, my colleagues made the day bearable. To this day I am friends with a lot of my coworkers so that is a plus.

Yelp Do Better

review_title: It is good for short term or if you thrive in a hustle environment
review_text: Training is fun and you get a healthy challenge with a lot of cheerleaders on the team. After you’re on the sales floor, you’re expected to hit your quota line every 3 months. If you fall below you’re put on a plan and if you miss the goal on the plan you’re terminated. Does not matter how long you’ve been there or how much you’ve earned the company. The better you do in your role, the higher those standards go, and that is why the job is unsustainable long term unless you thrive in that high pressure month to month structure. Managers get pushy the longer you’ve been there.

review_title: Great company,  but high turn over rate, not an actual CSM job.
review_text: Great company, values, and benefits. The job is technically a call center representative role, not your usual Customer Success Manager position. Daily responsibilities are to take 15+ inbound calls everyday, maintain a book of 90+ accounts and have a retention percentage of 55% or higher or else you will be put on a performance improvement plan with unrealistic goals. This job is meant for people who can multitask, aren’t phased when business owners are constantly yelling at you saying how much the sales reps misled them. You will get yelled at every beginning of the month and end of the month. Business owners are paying $500- $6k a month for advertising, and we aren’t able to help with reviews that aren’t being shown. The company needs to reevaluate their non-recommendation software - this has caused a lot of highly valued clients to cancel their advertising because we can’t do anything about reviews that aren’t being shown. Again the company is amazing, I loved it - but this role in particular and the CS department needs work. Stop giving unrealistic goals to your CSMs, and if you’re going to add more job responsibilities to your CSMs like have them be collections/finance, marketing consultants, and sales reps in one role, increase the salaries or else you will lose talented and skilled individuals.

My time at Yelp I learned a lot as it was my first sales position. You’ll be doing a lot of outbound cold calls. (80-120). Calling small businesses many of whom have strong feelings about Yelp. Not positive feelings. This is a low pay position but the benefits are pretty good. The businesses you’ll call have been called by Yelp dozens of times. If you’re just starting out this may be a good way to go. My sales managers were very good.

review_title: Great as a new job, not for long term
review_text:
This is a great company to start your career in sales but not many realistic opportunities for growth. They have a good training program. The pay is not great at 37k starting salary if you are needing to support yourself. 
A typical day is making 80 cold calls, have 2 hours of talk time, pitching twice, and closing once a day. Manager are able to track metrics throughout the day and listen to your calls. Team are about 10-15 people. There isn’t much culture since it is fully remote. 
You do need to have thick skin and be mentally strong, not only for dealing with customers you are selling to but also for accepting feedback from your manager. Each manager is different. The worst managers are micromanagers and pass their stress onto the team. My mental health has had some low lows due to this job, but I stuck with it for tenure and eventually the base salary increased to a more livable wage.

The only good thing is when you know how to sell the yelp ads being persuasive and get paid. But the pressure everyday can be overwhelming . They mislead their reps and business owners and the outcome is very bad for both parties involved. Toxic culture.

review_title: One of the Best Places to Work
review_text: Different departments have different responsibilities, but all have the same workload, maybe some more than others. You will have a lot of work to do and typically management is very understanding of that. I was grateful to have wonderful managers that were transparent and kind. Culture is amazing and I wish I participated more in the monthly activities. If you’re on the phones it can be stressful because apart of your compensation and job schedule is determined by sales.

This was my first sales gig as they accept entry level candidates. The company itself seems awesome to work for, but the account executive role is NOT for everyone. Generally you start with a training team and manager. You’ll lose the majority of your team within 6 months and training managers are usually great people but bad managers since they are learning as well. You must hit your numbers and closing enough deals to support a decent lifestyle in my opinion is difficult from month to month. If you have a great territory you can earn nice commission, but during territory swaps you may get a very rural area and see a big drop in deals closed. Things I really didn’t like was the pressure management places on you if you miss your quota. It’s never because your territory is bad, but always somehow your fault. They’ll tell you that you changed the approach that was working for you or just read their script ( which is super corny). They’ll try to guilt trip you for using your pto if you aren’t at quota, and you’ll find yourself working off the clock to catch up. I have friends in sales so this doesn’t seem to be specific to Yelp, but these are things that taught me the role wasn’t for me. They will stress you to no end and randomly feed you words during your calls unless you are a superstar. Every team seems to have one to two of those. 
The base pay is low and the way up is to stick around long enough to progress through pay levels. If you are fresh out of college or live on a lower income then you can have happiness here. It is a good company. If you are looking to make money, give yourself six months- you’ll know if you have IT or not by then. 
As for the product- it’s simply too expensive for many of the businesses you will call. It will work well for some and not so well for others. Business owners will have heard stories or be fed up with your calls by the time you speak with them and for this reason most of them won’t hear you out. Unfortunately, as someone who has used online ads for years I can say no matter what they tell you, the cost per click makes competitors more attractive outside of the restaurant industry. You need to be aggressive to sell this product well and one call close.

review_title: Great company with an amazing culture with perks for people who want to start a Sales career
review_text:
I am writing this with total transparency and honesty.  I enjoyed working with my colleagues at Yelp. Last year I was referred by an employee who had great things to say about Yelp. 

The training was very impressive to me and I decided to stay on and give this a shot. I have 25+ years of experience in the advertising industry. While we were required to make 80 calls a day and manage up,  I felt the ripple effect happening from Senior management and they started to crack down and micromanage me about my performance when in fact, I was meeting my quotas and performance requirements. 


 I had to switch managers in January because I wanted to grow and develop myself. While this did happen, at times we were pushed to make 100+ dials a day. 

Also we were given Stale accounts to call which never panned out. Also, customers who requested to be on the DNC list never were put into the DNC list and sent back to us to call. I was told several  times to put them into Inactive Pursuit. 

This in my view is a violation of Federal Law to call customers who request to be on DNC list. I've had first hand experience with this in the solar industry in the past and this company I used to work for was shut down by the FTC.

Also, while Yelp stated that they pride themselves on an excellent work culture and balance, I was not allowed at times to take my Wellness days unless I gave two weeks advance notice. 

This in my view is unacceptable and Yelp needs to properly communicate this with their employees.

While working remote from home was great, I was not allowed to work offsite at a shared office space or an Internet cafe. 

I wish everyone all the best. Thank you!

review_title: It can be a good job if you get a good manager
review_text:
Yelp as a company is great, the initiatives they have to make the job fun and the perks are unlike any other company I have known. You get care packages on a quarterly bases. Monthly health/fitness stipend, caregiver and educational stipend which is great. 

Day to day, you are expected to make 80 dials, a lot of pressure from the directors onto the managers which then it trickles down to the reps. If you have a good manager, the job is bearable. Working with a team is great, everyone is quite supportive between reps on a team, met some great people and friends.

The downside is there is very little training for managers to deal with the mental aspect of the job. You deal with a lot of businesses owners who have tried the program and felt like they were lied to. The script is very fluffed to make it seem like the program is going to fulfill the business "need" which leads to the belief the program will work better than it actually does but it is a slow burning program that may work. Managers will tell you to continuously keep calling even after you are told no. Managers will also not approve "do not call" requests so you will eventually see the same accounts come through and have to call again. Very few managers actually care for progression, they took out the human aspect of the job and will push you to get numbers. Those that perform get rewarded with more accounts which allows for more opportunities to sell the program so do not be fooled by those top sellers, they have more opportunities exponentially. Those who are not performing are typically pushed out to another manager which a lot of times leads to the manager letting the AE fail out and be fired. 
Very very few managers that will actually do their jobs and send you accounts, they are supposed to listen in and help during a call but they're stretched thin depending on the team. 

Managers are promoted based on their numbers and if they can sell. Just because somone is good at their own job of selling does not mean they are ready to be leaders of teams themselves.  Sure they have to help "coach" someone but thats a whole lot easier to help 1 person rather than a whole team. They should definitely have new manager shadow managers before they get their own teams of new hires. You can be on a manager track and still be let go because of performance months later just because you got moved to the wrong team.

Overall, very very few managers who are actually truly amazing and make the job worth it. Unless you are liked by the manager or are a strong performer, you will struggle and end up being pushed out. Not an easy job but doable, just have to do it in a way where you feel like you are actually helping the business owner.

Great benefits but the job itself was very high pressure sales and tedious. The managers had to listen to your calls all day everyday and if they thought you were getting a good lead they would barge in and talk to you while talking to the customer
Really hard work with cold calling, but they make up for it in benefits and a fun atmosphere. Some managers are amazing- you’ll learn so much and some managers are just absolutely terrible.
Training is great for someone who has never done sales before. Managers are there to support in every way possible. Many benefits that make it worthwhile

review_title: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
review_text:
You start out with full benefits day 1. You get a good amount of PTO. The training is pretty good. Most managers are trying to help you succeed.

100% cold calling. They want 80 calls with 2 hours of talk time. Most of your day is talking to a voicemail. They demand you leave voicemail and email at every dial (which causes the business to hate Yelp)

You are assigned a territory... and most of these businesses have been beat down for years with Yelp calls. Getting a sale happens most when a business newly claims a page. Not many per month.

It is very hard to make good money. You get an ok base pay and great benefits for a reason.

Working from home is great. Developing grit will better you. It will fry most people down within 6 months. Not a good long-term job but good to learn the game of sales.

I can only say good things about the company itself - every single manager is amazing, benefits are amazing, pay isn’t bad. The job itself can be stressful and in order to be successful you need to give 100% of your mental energy everyday and it take a toll.

review_title: Yelp, a fantasy. In the worst way possible
review_text: It was fine as a first sales gig, I would say I like my peers and your destiny at the company is dictated by your 1) territory and 2 manager. Overall experience has been very very hit and miss. 2/5.

I applied to this position because I used the app for several years and based on the application saying I would be working with local businesses by assisting them to use their listing to generate whatever led them over to our platform sounded like a win-win. Unfortunately this position is anything but that. You have to  cold call around 80 businesses a day to try to sell advertising to them so most of the businesses you call aren’t  expecting  your call and don’t want to get another sales call.You’re told in training that we are helping these businesses succeed and get them some more revenue through our advertising campaign but honestly the platform doesn’t work for every business and we’re still supposed to tell them that it does. You will get in  trouble with your managers if you stop calling accounts that ask you to because you’re not being persistent enough and if you’re not making the company any money you’re kind of a non-factor. The uncapped commission is a joke. So if that’s a selling point for you beware because you’ll be making the comps by a lot of revenue and your commission check won’t look like it. It’s pretty easy to move up in the company as long as you are a really good at sales and get a lot of revenue then you’ll be promoted pretty quickly but if you have a conscience and don’t want to lie and pester businesses every day you’re probably going to struggle at this role. review_title: Fun workplace, the culture is young and outgoing
review_text:
I was an Account Executive (aka cold caller/sales). I initially went into the position knowing very little about the company. I didn't expect much from the role considering I knew it was a sales position. 

The workday consisted of a team meeting from 8:30-9 am every day (manager discrepancy) then from 9-12 am you call and try to sell advertising. 12-1 PM is lunch, then 1PM-1:15 PM is another meeting (again, manager discrepancy), and then from 1-5 PM you call and try to sell some more. Day in and day out it is the same routine. You get 2 15-minute breaks but if you are not hitting your numbers, you are sort of looked at as "slacking off" if you take the breaks.

The first 6 months were the hardest, as you continually experience failing and getting shut down via phone. Of course, there are outliers but generally speaking, it takes 6 months to get comfortable on the phone and start selling really well. 

My manager was one of the best managers I knew. He genuinely cared for us, the team. He would always meet with us individually to see how we are doing and how he can help. Besides him, there were a few managers that I liked, but others were very numbers-oriented so they didn't care about "feelings" as much but more so performance. 

I did enjoy the people I met. The workplace culture is really new and young. I was 22 at the time so I was fresh out of college, looking to grow. I fit right within a majority of my coworker's age range. Yelp was also very inclusive to everyone, in all aspects. 

Yelp offered free "food" and beer. The "food" was sandwich meat and ramen along with bagels and cream cheese/jelly. Small stuff such as crackers and bags of chips. So technically yes, food, but not really. They also offered free beer from kegs for when you finish the day. In the beginning, I loved free beer, but then it got old coming to work the next day after drinking on a Tuesday night after a stressful day.

I didn't even last one month at Yelp. One of the worst jobs I have ever had although it was not the worst ever. Managers will blame you for thier own mistakes which I always took videos and pictures to prove that he was wrong. When shown he was wrong he would not take accountability and blame it on someone else. I understand micromanagement needs to happen to meet goals but the micromanagement that was implemented on me was for circumstances out of my control. For example, IT issues. IT will literally tell you the system is down but then you are talked down to by your manager for this. I asked for coaching for sales but was ignored or told to figure it out. I asked for coaching on other processes but was told to figure it out. This company is extremely unorganized. I'll give another example I was sent two packages with my work equipment. We will see if they compensate me correctly on my last check. There are many other negatives about this job but I already wrote enough. I highly recommend look at all of the other negative reviews about this company and avoid it.

Overall, its a decent company to work for, depending on who your manager is. The key problem while there was the misinformation some sales reps would give the customer about the advertising program. The company has changed their approach, so hopefully it leads to a better customer experience. Also, considering the amount of work that was done for a CSM, the compensation was not enough, by a long shot.

Once you complete the training which is like a few months long, you are rolled out to a new team with a new manager, which decides your fate at the company. Good luck. 
I had a great training manager and a few not so great managers afterwards.

review_title: Good culture, mediocre outlook, disappointing maturity level
review_text:
I started a career in sales with Yelp and stayed for a long time due my ability to adapt to the work-life balance at Yelp, and my ability to stay out of the office politics. During my time there, I saw many managers, directors, and high-performers come and go for various reasons, and the roll-out and highly-touted debut of many new territory formats, pricing structures, and ad models at Yelp. 

I could write a long essay of thoughts and takeaways of my time at Yelp, but I'll try to distill it to a few main points. 

First, Yelp's pay is sub-standard for the tech/internet space, but their benefits are comparatively much better than what you'll receive at most other companies. Healthcare, vision, dental, and gym reimbursement are excellent, maternity/paternity leave policy is AMAZING, 401k match is meh, stock programs are meh (possibly more on that later). Healthcare is one of those thing you don't appreciate until you really need it, and they totally have you covered on all fronts - you and dependents. That's one of the things Yelp does REALLY well.

Second, Yelp's pay is probably slightly lower than what you can make at other major software/tech/internet companies while being better than what you can make in many call-center operations, but the level of stress and the output demands are high. Because Yelp's client turnover is high and their pricepoints are low, expect to be micromanaged towards high output (dials, talktime, etc) with the hopes of high production and results. Individual commission are small, so you must "stack" tons of small deals in order to make good money. In order to make the deals, you will need to do a ton of work and make a ton of calls and figure out what works for you. Because you're selling ad subscriptions that many clients don't stay with very long, there's an incentive to command, confuse, or 'promise the moon' in order to the client to sign and put in their CC info - and then to cut and run, leaving the client to figure out what's next. The incentives to sell are so high that in the time I was in sales at Yelp, around 50% of the extreme sales overproducers were eventually terminated after management discovered some loophole, gimmick, promise, or untrue line they were using that outright violated the rules and left the company exposed. 

Third, as far as outlook on the company, I have two thoughts. 

First outlook point is is that Yelp has historically been slow to bring needed products and updates to market, and this has only changed (slightly) in the past 2 years. Anecdotally, around 2016 my sister-in-law told me "I like Yelp, but every time I visit it, the layout looks it hasn't been updated in four years." She was right. Around then, they started working on being more responsive and concerned with consumer-appeal, because there had been a slight flatlining in usage. One of their company values is "protect the source" - and that can mean protecting the product and site so closely that they are slow to implement change, and do it too slowly to catch market opportunities. This has effected their stock price and ability to innovate. Yelp was one of the last companies in the space to unveil a cost-per-click model (which clients had been arguing about for years) and they've only recently (in the last 2-3 years) started to be more attentive to consumers and salespeople, in rolling out tools to make them more effective. 

Last point on outlook is that despite whatever gains they make, Yelp is and will always be constrained within the limits of a business model that is, on the whole, unappealing to a high percentage of business owners. Yelp essentially publishes opinions about businesses -- There is nothing proprietary or unique about that business model except the user community, which is shrinking due to lots of competition from Google Local reviews, Facebook, Instagram, and the like. And within the market, positive reviews are awesome and can significantly lift a business' revenues - but restaurants and businesses earn that with a TON of "offline" hard work, knowledge, and sweat, while negative reviews are so upsetting to business owners, that if one overly-opinionated reviewer says some extremely negative comments (or allegations) about a business, it can turn the business owner completely against Yelp and can kill any deal they'd ever make to advertise. 

Yelp is constrained within a business model that is in many ways unnecessary and unappealing to most business owners. That fact alone makes it a tough sale for an employee/rep, and an even tough business to grow meaningfully. During my time at Yelp they were consistently trying to sell the business but could never find a deeply interested buyer. Yelp will probably always be the way they are because they've chosen a very difficult problem to solve, and there may not be enough opportunity in it for you to make the money you really want to.

Stressful and high-pressure, however hugely depends on the team you get placed on a subsequent manager you have. This is cold calling sales, super gritty and challenging but excellent training provide. Tip: believe in the product

Management isn't the best, the managers don't know how to lead, all they care about are their team numbers and not development. The product doesn't work for every business you call, but they want you to shove it and force in down businesses throats.

I worked at Yelp for about 2.5 years and overall had an average experience. The job is very monotonous - you have a meeting in the morning with your team, you hop on the phone for 4 hours (get yelled at, hung up on and cursed at), have lunch, have another meeting and repeat the same thing. You get lucky to have a couple good conversations a day. Businesses owners are tired of hearing from Yelp. 

Work environment is a plus. Coworkers are fun and managers have a lot of energy. Work environment is what kept me there for over 2 years.

I worked at the Yelp Chicago office for a year and a half. I was one of the few people who successfully made it through training. Favoritism is huge at Yelp. If you don’t hit double your monthly number you are looked down on. Pressure is unbearable and the sales acumen they teach is extremely sketchy language. The directors and office head will continually talk down to people and managers. My manager and director both tried to use intimidation to get me to quit (they did not want to carry my quota another month) because I was honestly and open about looking for another job. College grads beware.
I happened to be fortunate to have a great manager. Intense working environment "hustling". Nice perks stock options, snacks, baristas, beer taps, happy hours and amazing company culture.

I loved it when I first started in person but COVID really ran down the daily operations at Yelp. Distributing work from home equipment was less than perfect, and I had major troubleshooting issues with it. There was an incessant need to check in with managers to the point that I spent more time on the phone with managers than the clients I had in my pipeline. Some managers even expected us to use our personal cell phone numbers to reach out to clients which I felt was a big no-no for a few reasons. For my pipeline specifically it was extremely hard to sell (NY/NJ/MI area) because of Yelp's response to COVID. Many businesses closed (for good or temporarily) and I was often told by business owners that advertising was not even a priority. Also Yelp needs better damage control ESPECIALLY with people who leave untrue comments or just straight up threatening comments on business pages. I was told there is software they use to prune through these comments but I had one client who I was trying to sell to that had a comment that has remained on their business page for years accusing them of being a terrorist (and many other foul things). I too thought it was unacceptable but the comment was never removed. There was nothing I could do on my end, yet I was still expected to sell to this person! Thankfully the business owner saw the value in having Yelp but I felt so bad that I couldn't help him. He wanted this issue addressed before spending any other monies with us because that one comment alone affected his business reputation greatly. While I had some positive relationships with clients, I had too many clients who had a similar issue like this one guy.

The place is super nice and appealing with a coffee bar and games and off-site activities but if you value your mental health or are a woman, like myself, don’t work there. It’s kinda like highschool or Tinder there, everyone tries to date everyone and harass you- with no consequences. I was there for about a year and I lost my mind!!! It’s a great gig and job if you have a good manager. Chicago is notorious for bad, arrogant managers that will bully you so if you get one of those like me you’ll be driven out. By bullying. Anyway it’s free coffee, some friends, yummy snacks, great location. Cold calling is fun cause people love or hate yelp and you gotta sell it. Don’t let managers tear you down! There are insane characters that do this job, beware.
Really helped to jump start my career in sales and life as a whole! All the managers are there to help you grow and succeed! I would recommend this opportunity to anyone!

I find that at a company like this it is for the young just starting out. I feel that once my manager found out that I owned a couple of buildings that she began to have a problem with me. She didn't understand I was older I wasn't trying to get established I was just looking to go in a different direction with my career After that I feel it was her mission to fire me. She began eliminating me from all the extra training that people at my time and level were getting and she just all of sudden stopped communicating or even speaking with me. 

Then I got sick and called off and she stated that I was tardy and I was on some list and she and her friend from HR called me at home and let me go. Even when I showed her the slip from the Metra train being late I was still put on an attendance list. She just did not care for me and got to the point where she didn't hide it. So all is well life goes on but I should have switched teams.

review_title: Great Pay but management brags about picking favorites
review_text:
Pay is great and commission is reasonable and good too. Amazing work and life balance.
 
Managers play favorites. Higher performing reps also play favorites. 
If you don't fit into the "click" people will ignore you, shame you and gossip negative things about you. 

Multiple managers and reps sleep together then don't report the relationship to HR so they can get to stay on the same team and exchange the newer/hotter accounts between each other. 

Operations Managers bragg about how it's like being in a college fraternity still and they wont help employees grow or succeed when they don't fit into that group. 

I've never been more bullied, isolated, ignored and shamed by managers and coworkers before. Felt like I being in high school again except I didn't fit in here.

They fired over 700 people and laid off 1000 people in March 2019 with no notice due to Covid 19. So job security isn't a thing here. 

Top performing reps on my team and my manager would tell me often that I wasn't welcome in their group chats even though I was apart of their team. I felt very isolated, bullied and shamed because of this. 

Very unkind, unhealthy and uncomfortable company to work because of the kind of people they choose to have around. 

Sales tactics are manipulating, fear driving and exceedingly pushy on business owners. 

HR ignores/doesn't take it seriously when you report these problems. 

Great pay and benefits. Unhealthy and horrible culture to work in.

review_title: Strong favoritism and discrimination, high school atmosphere
review_text: "Yelp Kool-Aid" is a real thing. Stocked kitchen and kegs after work drew you in. Once you settle in, you'll start to notice the culture is terrible. There is discrimination is all aspects (age, gender, race, what school you went to, what sorority/fraternity you were in, etc.). You advance and get favored if your manager likes you (based on the above criteria). This includes better/bigger territories, promotions, etc. They claim that they believe in work/life balance, when truly, as a manager, we were given tasks to do OUTSIDE of work on our own time almost every day. We were required to show up extremely early and stay extremely late to get things done. I would often get criticized for using PTO or sick days, even though I never went over my allotted balance. The expectations as a manager were extremely unrealistic, and the compensation definitely made it not worth it. If you have sales experience, I highly recommend that you DO NOT work here. You will be brain washed, with upper management telling you to blame everything on yourself and that everything that goes wrong is your own fault. They don't care about their people, not one bit. Oh, and one last thing: They laid off people via a pre-recorded video with 0 days notice, 0 transparency.

I really enjoyed building loyalty with local businesses, however it was eventually overshadowed by manipulative management. I did enjoy the company overall, but my management team made me hate my life.

Often I was tasked with work that was not in my job description because "it showed initiative and would help me get a full time position" or it was a "new skill I just have to learn". Eventually I realized I was doing most of my managers work in addition to my own. I got a pay cut and hours cut, I was able scrape by just because of that full time promise. There's so many more shady things I don't even have time to disclose here... 

The final nail in the coffin was when I realized three different viable full time positions were not even mentioned to me, I was not even given the chance to apply. 

After two years, I realized that I would never get the option to work full time, and gave up. Again, I would work for the company, but I'm scared from management.
The pay sucks for such a huge company. I felt like I was in grade school from the treatment of the managers. Communication passed down from managers are not consistent.

review_title: Beat place ever, the work is hard but you are not gonna come acroos a place like Yelp if you get in take advantage of  your co-workers and managers
review_text: Great place, fun incentives! kegs!! fun HARD WORK but the perks definitly makes up for the job. If you have a negative outlook in life or the smallest things ever you willl stick out like a sore thumb take advantage of a great place, truly miss this job  covid devastated this place. Everyone stay safe

As the CSM your job is putting out fires lit by sales. Yelp uses shady and unethical sale practices to sell a product that seldom works. You get to deal with the mess. Majority of the inbound calls are from frustrated, angry and disappointed business owners who have no idea what they paid for and what they got. Now as a CSM it’s your job to educate these business owners about the products and platform the only problem is it seldom works it’s fine for restraints and nightlife but other than that nobody really searches Yelp for professional services yet all these biz seem to max out their budget every month without getting jack all which begs the question what is up with yelps impressions and clicks how is a business getting so many clicks yet not a single paying customer I see this all the time which obviously leads to a lot of anger with ROI issues but we are just suppose to reassure them that no yelp works you are getting clicks that means people are interested total bs and then there are the reviews that get filtered oh boy that’s another ball game good luck with that convo. It will feel like a dead end job you do a million things don’t get paid enough burnout rate is high get use to being cussed out and yelled at a lot on the phones. Management is pretty inept the managers job is to resell yelp to you because if you have any sense you soon realise it’s pretty much a scam and the managers are all brainwashed kool aid drinking zombies. Mind you I am actually a top performer in my role and I like my manager as a person but boy those robotic responses of his lol. My advice stay away call center jobs suck anyways this is probably one of the worst out there. It’s not that the culture is particularly bad it’s just the nature of the job. I also feel bad for our sales people who are forced to sell using vague verbiage so that they can swindle business owners to putting their cards on file. Like I said yelp is an ok place culture wise but the nature of the job sucks. Good luck if you do join most don’t last long and I don’t know how long I can take I. 
platform

This is a job you'll take fresh out of college. The benefits are great but that's the only reason why people stay and because of the friends they make while working there. There's no culture, they don't care about the employees, SOME managers don't know what they're doing. I can go more in depth but please if you are 25+ this job is not for you! There are better jobs out there.

well i don't really have much to say. the job was great just not what i am looking to do long term. they take good care of you and let you know whats expected early on. high intensity job, great people. loved 2/3 of my managers.

review_title: Nonexistent job security, toxic, sickeningly fake environment
review_text: worked at yelp for 6 months before my manager fired me on an impulsive, bipolar whim. Everyone at yelp is so fake it’s actually repulsive. You’re not permitted to show any emotion whatsoever beside happiness. We would spend all day harassing business owners, pushing a product that 90 percent of the time didn’t work, looking for the next sucker to manipulate. I was a yelp elite prior to this role. I loved yelp. But i will never use it again and I never clicked on the sponsored results because they weren’t relevant to what I was searching for. I still brought the company a TON of money and was a top performing rep. But one day my manager decided to fire me because she was emotionally unstable and the company completely turned their backs on me. I’ve never felt more betrayed.

I will say that if you are placed with a manager that's a good fit and fosters a positive team environment, the job can be more than tolerable. THAT BEING SAID, I was placed with a manager where we butted heads and I requested a team change multiple times with evidence as to why to both my director and HR and all I got told was to work on communication with said manager. This turned into a hostile environment and if I had been moved from said team, I might still be there. 

TLdR; trust the reps to know what's best for them!

review_title: Had all the fixings of a Silicon Valley company in midtown Manhattan.
review_text: Manager style varies immensely but the the pressure to perform can be immense while you are making 100+ calls and getting hung up on 100 times a day. A glorified boiler room.

review_title: Great place to work and learn cold call sales skills
review_text: They really help you develop your skills as a salesperson. One of the best sales training programs across industries. Sometimes the managers can harp a little too much on "daily metrics" but cold call sales is a numbers game so you get what you signed up for.

The people and the culture at Yelp are awesome, but it’s hard to maintain stamina in the AE role. The deal cycle is very quick here, and because of that you’re always being pushed to do more. Most people won’t get promoted either, there are many more AE’s than there are managers.

First benefits are impeccable!! Free lunch breakfast and snacks and drinks !! Loved it ! That alone made it hard to leave Yelp. To be honest it was great at the beginning and I stayed as long as I could but I couldn’t anymore , managers are constantly hounding you to make more calls and people constantly hanging up on you got so tired and old and it wears on your psyche after a while. I really didn’t enjoy going to work and was constantly waking up and wishin g I didn’t have to go face the day and no one should live like that day after day!

This is a good place for broke college kids with no sales experience. Your managers are basically kids as well. Free food... to keep up from not falling asleep because you are on the phone harassing people for 8 hours straight. Coffee.soda. 50 cent ramen noodles, chips, cereal, string cheese. No thank you, I don’t need diabetes. They say you are uncapped commission. But there’s a catch. these so called leads are recycled so these leads have already been reached out 3 to 8 times already. They’ll hype you about the good moments which any job would. But most of these businesses honestly don’t need you to sell the Yelp App. They honestly don’t care about you cause they already hired 60 people for the following month. If you miss the frat and sorority life then this is the job for you. To eat college food and drink beer after 5 and be on the phone for 8 hours. 80 percent of you calls is people hanging up on you. To make matters even better the big sales pitch for bigger companies are held to other sales people so they make more commission.
Rejection from customers and tough to get through to them. Advancement is based on sales performance but managers do help out with advice and encouragement.

review_title: Good place to work if you're are looking for communication and beginner sales skills
review_text:
I have worked at Yelp NYC for a year now. And I have honestly been disappointed. There are some extremely good sales people here that are letting their talent go to waste at this company. The product is only ok, and definitely not the best like they preach. People here think that they are "marketing experts" when really they have no idea what effective marketing is. It's honestly so sad to see so many good people fall for this company and believe everything management and executives here say. Literally, most of the sales managers here have absolutely no knowledge on what legitimate marketing is. 

The majority of consumers that have joined our platform feel scammed, and had NO ROI. Let me repeat, NO ROI. 

All I can say is, If you're an individual who is looking for beginner sales skills then you will find it here. Everything beyond that is trash and how the sales managers and directors sell their employees on this ineffective platform is extremely sad. Also not to mention, this place is like a frat house. For example, I've seen managers walk on desks and fool around. They have awful incentives that really don't benefit you at all. They will take all most half of your commission as well. So be careful not to be sold on their commission structure.

If you're a TRUE professional this place is NOT a place to consider. There are better companies out there. Yelp has an awful reputation, just look it up or ask someone who has worked with Yelp before. You could probably walk into a local business wherever you are located and ask how they feel about Yelp.

review_title: If u have tough skin & a strong desire to succeed in sales, Yelp is for u
review_text: Yelp hires hard core telemarketers or â€œaccount executivesâ€ by the hundreds & slowly fires them when they don’t meet quota. Only the successful who sell survive. So if you want to be in a culture of that hanging over your head daily, go for it. They do have micro managers guiding their teams. They also have good supportive culture, great benefits & location. If you love sales, tech & Yelp, you might succeed. If not, go elsewhere.

review_title: It's just fraternity and sorority kids out of College for the most part
review_text: I was excited to work for this company. I'm used to face-to-face sales but I figured the culture would fill the gaps for me. Here's my take. Training was like college. Actually, no. Maybe high school. Your managers in training are also training, so get ready for that if you're coming from a company where you were once a manager and realized they're off on their leadership skills. Two months in, you go to the vet org and people who trained you will treat you differently. My new manager completely went from being cool to being a micro managing a-hole. Targeted me when he wanted to make an example over things that were minuscule. I had a sit down with him MULTIPLE times as to why I seem like I have an attitude. (If you're not a bubbly person, expect people to ask you if you're okay every 30 minutes) They have this smile and dial mentality. I'm there to work, not to smile every ten seconds. If you're right out of college, this job is a good stepping stone but if you're someone like me who has been in hard sales working alongside older professionals, the day to day environment will get to you. There is a high turnover rate for a reason, you call businesses that have already been solicited for years before you got assigned and all that pent up resentment toward the company is dropped on you when you call, and you need to call them over and over as it pops up in your timeline. Your manager will barge your calls and tell you what to say in your headset, but if they barge you late and don't know how your tone was or the rapport you built, the pushy sales tactic will cost you the deal and they will tell you what YOU did wrong. (Why hire us if you don't let us be us on the phone?) I was promised I'd get a new territory after hitting quota two months in a row but my manager switched up what he said to me once I asked about it, made it seem like it was miscommunication but that was nonsense because I had confirmed it with him the moment he told me about it. Another thing, don't listen to that. The few friends I've made there explained their managers changed their territories and didn't need to hit quota. It seemed like me asking for help was a nuisance in comparison to another team member doing so. I found the job tedious, but if the day to day soliciting doesn't bother you and you're okay with sitting or being in one spot, kudos. Pay structure, hmmm. You only become commission eligible after hitting 30k, then you need to hit 12k for that month to actually get anything. at 12k, your commission is $150 and 100 after that. You get your commission checks every month, just know taxes on them rip you. Again... Collegiate level. Things work best if your territory is good, or your manager. If both suck, then you won't succeed and you will need to speak to your director about either switching teams or getting a new territory. This place is VERY MICRO MANAGED. If you're not used to having someone hovering over you from when you come in and when you leave, DON'T TAKE THIS JOB!!!

review_title: Free coffee ... and that's about it
review_text:
I worked at Yelp as an AE in Washington, DC. The Yelp culture is FUN in your 2 months of training. Very young employees.

Management is HORRIBLE. Barely trained and always playing favorites. Everyone HAS to take lunch between 12-1, even though HR insists you can go anywhere between 10-2 -- good luck telling your manager that.
My most recent manager was nasty, and had 5+ HR complaints filed but nothing was done about it. 

A truly toxic workplace where they LIE about the commission structure and the only advancement is from Sales person to Sales manager (a promotion they give to people who have only been working for as little as 7 months). Also, you sit in your chair for 8 hours and if you get up you have to tell your manager where you're going (is this middle school?). You harrass small businesses by calling them 2+ times weekly for months on end.

The turnover rate is HIGH. My training class in August of 2018 had about 60 people, now, in August of 2019 there are maybe 15 of those people still working.

NOT a place I'd recommend, in fact, avoid Yelp like the plague. I submitted my 2 weeks notice and they ended up taking me aside and saying "today is going to be your last day" without warning or pay. What kind of company treats employees like that?

review_title: This place is like a sweatshop
review_text: The benefits at Yelp are insane.  But once you get out of training you quickly realize that 95% of business owners HATE Yelp- as well they should. You'll get 2 cities to call that more than likely are very small.  Business owners have been getting called by yelp since they day they signed up.  The yelp script is 5 pages most of which can be thrown away.  Also yelp's stats go on assumption of sales for your customer not the actual truth.  There is a reason that every month this company brings on 50-60 new reps.  Your manager will go up and down the row and is a literal cheerleader since they know the job sucks so bad.  In the 6 or so months I was there I saw 4 people in with security and the paramedics due to the high stress.

Felt like I sold my soul to the devil. Felt like I was doing the devil's work. Managers were horrible for the most part. They repeat each others' words like they were brainwashed. Not a safe place. I hated going to this job every day.

I have been at Yelp for over 3 years. I have completed their Leadership Development Programs. I have had revenue months higher than many managers and still don’t see a future here. Yelp is a very â€œyoungâ€ company. The managers are young, inexperienced in management, and lack basic soft skills. The reps on the floor often haven’t held other jobs in their lives. But the issue with Yelp is deeper than this. Let me dive in:

Yelp, originally, was a fantastic place to work. The opportunities were high, the culture was fun (but not overbearing), and the pressure and pace of work was manageable. When Yelped switches to non term contracts, or RASS, things changed drastically. Quotas stayed the same, but deal sizes were extremely smaller (1/8th of the maximum size of the old product deal size). This meant that all of a sudden you had to work harder to get less and hopefully reach a quota that many struggle to hit. To make matters worse, with the new program chargebacks increased company wide. This meant that if you did make a commission you can expect that money to be taken away because advertisers you signed up turned off their ads earlier than predicted. Overall, it’s a power play by Yelp to appear to have a larger market share of the local environment but also not pay out as well. At least this is the experience I and many others have observed. 

As mentioned, Yelp management lacks soft skills. I’ve watched managers tell representatives that unless they make 120 dials (double the old expectations) that they will not get promoted. I’ve watched management tell employees that their diseases or age will hold them back, or tell other managers this when they think they’re in safe spaces. I’ve watched coworkers dive into depression due to unrealistic expectations and crushing pressure brought on by micromanaging, overburdened and undertrained management. 

You also have a culture that is very forced. If you don’t attend after work happy hours you are looked down upon. If you aren’t out drinking until 4 am with coworkers you’re ostracized. If you’re not railing adderall or coke in the bathroom 4 times per day in the stalls you’re probably getting depressed. Yes, this actually happens more often than Yelp acknowledges. 

As far as pay- it’s well below industry standard. And once you get to the Senior level your salary stops rising but your quota doesn’t. You’re expected to produce more and work harder but don’t get correlating pay.

Yelp can be good. Right now it is not.

I didn't have the kind of personality to succeed in this role because I felt bad asking people to take time out of their day and listen to me. But it was an excellent introduction to sales.

They lay amazing groundwork, give you lots of encouragement and tons of opportunity for development. They'll accidentally teach you a lot about yourself and life generally. If you bring a good attitude, work hard and focus on the right things, you'll do well. They're nice people.

My main gripe is that the sales approach is just pushy sales wrapped in some nice language about being helpful by growing their business. We're taught to pivot into selling people rather than doing full account management. It can feel like you're tricking people into buying something they aren't even prepared to consider and don't understand. The company seems fine with that approach because it makes them money. It feels wrong for a product you need to trust to try. AND makes your job as a sales person very confusing.

You HAVE to be money-motivated to do well in this job. They say you don't, but I'm not and still quit even though the money was really good.  If you feel pressure to pay off debt quickly, want to take a vacation, have something you want to save for or another bigger dream, it's a great place. If your needs are simple and you're easily satisfied, it might not be a good fit.

I learned a lot here. I learned how to take responsibility for myself, what my potential might be and what it's like to get out what you put in. I learned to ask for what I need.

When I left the job in the spring of 2019, we were expected to make 80 calls, pitch twice and close 1 transaction in order to have a successful day. It's doable and it's also a grind. 
Usually there's a quick meeting in the morning and one in the afternoon. Meetings here always have a point and managers don't like to waste time.

The culture can be super sales bro-y, laid back, like a family or feel cubicle-y. It depends on what office, director or team you have what the day to day feeling is. Overall, the company is inclusive and hires people who hold that value closely. Women are well represented (management included) but people of color are not (yet). But, it's welcoming and you can feel the culture shifting.

Management is awesome. I cannot say enough good things about them. They work hard to develop and keep people there and don't like to let anyone who's a good worker go. They also don't keep bad managers and have heard about a couple of people who were not suited to leadership being asked to step back down to a sales role.

Hardest part of the job was getting people to listen to you. Accounts are over-called and have been burned by other companies and sales people who don't deliver on promises. 

The best things are the training and management. You learn a lot about yourself and are encouraged all along to be your best. They taught me my value as an employee.

I thoroughly enjoyed working at Yelp. I stepped into the office with little to no sales experience. Yelp's training program prepared me for my career. My managers and directors genuinely cared about my growth and success. There is always workplace culture.
Yelp has a ton of great employees and managers and offers a top notch benefits package. Fast paced work environment. Great sales training program and opportunity for advancement.

This job is not for an experienced sales person. The sale is very pushy management literally uses the line "Lets just turn this on and in a week if it doesn't work you can turn it off" any real sales person would never utter those words. Its a fun office they know how to hire great people. Very political office, my manager and I had a disagreement so I got set up with one of the worst territories in the country, I would make 100 calls and speak to 1 person. Average manager is 24 years old and immature, Its college 2.0

It can be awesome if you win at least 1 of the 2 Yelp lotteries, Manager and Territory. Otherwise you'll just hate the job. Yelp will make you more desirable to future employers.  

The executives have no Idea what they are doing and have no business being executives at a publicly traded company.

review_title: Wonderful company that values their employees, but the day-to-day is tough
review_text: Yelp did a great job of growing and developing their workplace culture. The environment is very fratty and overwhelmingly young so it can be easy to forget that you're in a professional work environment. There is a lot of opportunity for advancement so long as you're an effective salesperson and have a high average close rate. Everyone is gung-ho all the time and any kind of negative attitude is looked down upon to the point where the environment can feel incredibly fake. There's even a gong that people hit each time they close a deal. Looking back, it really was a wonderful experience; just not for me. I am a highly positive and motivated person, but there was a general lack of motivation at Yelp across the board likely due to the job's pressures and heavy mental toll. The performance-based nature of the position and manufactured positivity definitely did not help. People are often promoted quickly resulting in peers turning into managers - oftentimes before they're ready. Management is incentivized to keep reps on track and dissuade them from any potentially harmful thoughts or actions, so all the while, reps are being "sold" by their managers. The job often advertises itself as a marketing position, but don't let that fool you; it's straight up cold calling. There are metrics you are expected to hit each day in terms of call volume as well as other, more specific targets.

Cold-calling is hard, but with my team, my manager, and my perseverance I was able to learn and grow everyday.  The job is difficult, there are very high expectations set on you, but the people and workplace environment make it better.

review_title: Not for everybody. Fun place to work however, hard work low pay starting.
review_text:
READ ME!! Here is the full REAL scoop

First this is a job where its more about experience & the stamp on the resume. They act like you can make all this crazy amount of money but I sold 23k last month and commission check was less than 5% of that.

(YSDP) THEY LOCK YOU IN TO SALE YOUR FIRST 30K WITH NO COMMISSION STARTING OFF- Heads up.

They will NOT explain anything to you in training about how the structure works...and the structure needs work!! I have seen some people literally get finessed to keep in "YSDP" when in reality they sold the product however, the business cancelled after a month for example.


This job can be stressful right off the bat. The managers are GREAT however, the leadership, upper management you CANNOT trust. They say one thing  but really mean something else. I suppose it depends on your director that you fall under. Terrible leadership from my end. You''ll get an email from one of the top guys every single day trying to motivate you, but yet he will walk by you or by your desk and never say a word lol.

Pay: Just going to be real, for you really to making "good" commission money you need to sale like 20k a month which is about 650$ after taxes. Com. checks are taxed 40%!! Chargebacks pretty much happen every month which can be draining, cutting into your commission check. The pay is low starting off.

Incentives: Sell 200k "here's a wireless headset" sick bro!! 
 
Atmosphere:   It's on point..kitchens stocked with food and free cofe in the lobby....they do a awesome job hiring great people who can literally become friends with and make connections outside of work and broader your networking circle. They got music playing all day which helps keep good energy. Also ping pong,game room, pool table and A KEG!! 

BEWARE: The people you will be calling HATE YELP AND WILL HATE YOU.... they dont even know you and theyll hate you because of Yelp ... the sales are SUPER aggressive.

Yelp is also very sneaky . They lost a lot of money from their top investors and took a week out of pay from us and did it so sneaky.

YOU CANNOT TRUST UPPER MANAGEMENT OR THE STRUCTURE 

Great people that work here tho ...awesome managers!!

review_title: There is a certain type of person for this job. I wasn’t that.
review_text:
This job is for a very specific type of person. If you can stomach constantly bothering people who are trying to run a business, or enjoy negotiating with those same business owners for a 20 minute conversation while ensuring you meet all expectations, sales and otherwise then Yelp might the place for you. I personally should have never taken this job. It was a terrible fit for me and caused a great deal of stress so much so that it started to manifest into physical pain. You’re trained to ignore business owners objections and go into every single one of the expected 80+ class a day with the mentality that you have to sell this person. Your managers might tell you otherwise but it’s bs. I have only been with the company for three almost four months now and I am desperately trying to escape. I’m even considering doing Lyft or Uber as a place holder that’s how bad it’s gotten for me. 

There are some positives however. I actually enjoyed the company I worked for. Before deciding to move away from the company I was trying to move into their IT department so I can remain part of the team but contribute in a different way. That wasn’t possible so I out. Other pros include the free Yelp kitchen all employees have access to. Granted the options don’t change and you will get tired of them quickly. The benefits package is really nice. You don’t a dime for personal health, dental, and vision which is nice. The office is in the Merchandise Mart in downtown Chicago, and I personally enjoyed being downtown. If you don’t however looks elsewhere. My manager was cool but that will obviously vary depending on who you get. 

Overall the only way I could recommend this job to anyone is if that person meets the following criteria:

1. Don’t mind pestering people everyday (You’re managers will tell you it’s super important that biz owners talk to you, but relevance is subjective)
2. Can sit in your butt for 9 hours a day making phone calls to people who don’t want to talk to you. 
3. Are patient with the process and themselves. (Especially if this is first sales job you’ve ever had)
4. Can stomach how nasty some of the people you call can be. I’ve been cursed out, called names, etc... 
5. You absolutely have to be good a talking to people. It’s literally all you do. 
6. Can leave work at work and not bring it home. I struggled with this one personally just due to the sheer amount of stress this job put me under.

If you can’t stay true to these I wouldn’t touch this job with a 10ft pole
Amazing training program with strong support and mentoring from managers and directors. High volume outbound calls with a very transactional sales cycle.
In a nutshell, this job sucks!!!! You literally do the same thing every single day.  Managers are always down your throat because they have nothing better do.
Great place to work. The culture and environment during my time as an independent contractor was great. The supervisors and managers were very collaborative in making my work better.

review_title: Comany as a whole is great
review_text:
The company as a whole is great with a good outlook for the future. 
The Managers often give credit to others and not to those that work hard and often time for get about the people who have worked hard for years. 
Also, the crowd is a younger generation that is very sensitive to everything you say and will often time be offended by generally quiet people.

review_title: Absolute Nightmare to Work at Yelp
review_text:
There's no greater embarrassment or shame than working at Yelp. Your job is to sit in a sweatshop of telephones where you just call the same businesses over and over again while your manager lies to you about why you aren't closing deals.

You aren't closing deals because the territories have been called non-stop for years. The business owner may have even tried yelp before and canceled, however you still have to call them every other day for a month (at least). More often than not, the business owner is just sick and tired of yelp calling non-stop every other day for as long as they can remember. 

If you get a business owner on the phone who for some reason hasn't hung up on you immediately, your manager will make you yell at them and demand their credit card on the spot. No one in their right mind should purchase anything from someone who calls them out of the blue and demands them to put their credit card into their computer. But a fool and their money do go separate ways.

Additionally, you will be forced to hang out with some of the worst people you will ever encounter in your life. 90% of the employees are frat bros and sorority girls who have never worked a day in their life. Newsflash: this isn't a real job either.

Of the remaining 10% of potentially decent co-workers, you will make some friends. Your common bond of hating every single minute of every day of your work life will bring you close and you will get drinks with these people long after you leave yelp, like prisoners of war being re-united.

You will share stories about the time you were locked up at Yelp. You will laugh. And you will thank god you don't work there anymore.

Yelp has a pretty good culture but and a fun values like be unboring. I don't like the work at all. The product is sub par. There is no room for autonomy there. I like my manager and team members. The salary is poor. I don't see real opportunity for growth.

It was great to work for a company where people push you to be your best, and help you fight towards reaching your quota. My team and manager were always there for me when i needed them, and i was there for them when they needed me.

It's a great sales job, they have a wonderful training program, they are supportive, and the culture can be fun. Although they reiterate the importance of respecting sales prospects and recommending what is best for them, management does put pressure on employees to "do what ever it takes" to make the largest sum of money as possible each day, despite the fact that it might not be helpful to the sales prospect. They are supportive and recognize employee's hard work, but there is a tremendous amount of pressure put on managers and sales reps each month. That part of the job was unfortunate, but I did gain valuable experience in communications and marketing strategies.

review_title: Fun environment with coffee shop, kegs, and ping pong tables.
review_text: Great environment to dive headfirst into sales. Phenomenal training and a very supportive group around you. Everyone there is willing to teach you how to succeed.

review_title: Fun and upbeat work place with fully stocked kitchen
review_text: The only two down falls in this dream job we’re that it didn’t matter what time it was in your territory everyone has to come in, take lunch, and leave at the same time. My territory was 2 hours ahead so by the time 4pm rolled around I wouldn’t have anyone to call for the last hour and a half. The other downfall was that some teams switch a lot so as soon as you would get comfortable you got switched again, which could be see as a positive thing because you do meet new people and learn new things from new managers. Other than that the job is amazing you have free drinks, food, and snacks all day and they have AWESOME benefits. Yelp really is a dream job.

Yelp has a very fast paced telemarketing sales position where you start with the first 30 days, then promote to 60, 90 and then promote you to the floor to work your own leads and send you out in to "open waters" to pitch clients different sales packages. Yelp gives the right tools and managers customized to your strengths and weaknesses to help you thrive not only to grow your salary and commission but to also help businesses grow their wallets and philosophies.

review_title: Good place to develop sales skills
review_text: A typical dat at Yelp includes making about 80 cold calls a day. Your managers are constantly monitoring your metrics. It's a good place to develop one's sales skills. Your coworkers are overall very friendly. You work a 40hr work week, and they provide good health benefits.

Being presented with an opportunity for Yelp was awesome until the second week there. I had just graduated from college so I thought it was so great to find a job right away. First week is all training and they hype it up and make it sound awesome, while it's annoying to hear everyone speak like a valley girl, but they tell you not to speak that way on the phone. The second week, your'e cold calling and getting hung up on by everyone you call. Your manager "barges" in on your call and makes you say what they're telling you to say. You're trying to listen to the customer and your manager at the same time. It's not very effective. During the interview they made it seem like you would be working face to face with businesses and before you know it, they give you a headset and your getting hung up on all day. You're basically a telemarketer.

review_title: A good starting place for recent college grads, prepare to grind.
review_text:
I've been working at Yelp for a year and 8 months and during that time I've struggled to live on a very meager salary. The company culture still feels very immature and the leadership struggles to maintain a professional setting at the local sales level. At times it's too loose and feels like a college fraternity. Leadership ranges from managers that are raging alcoholics that hook up with their subordinates while on the other hand there will be managers that are heavy handed with micro managing people and incredibly ineffective with meetings. Since most of the employees are young and are charged with hormones it's no surprise that most employees do not separate boundaries of dating. Pay wise, most employees feel underpaid for amount of work they do and this is especially true for reps that speak multiple languages and take an additional unpaid account management role. The job is highly stressful because pay is dicey since there is a high rate of client churn and most of your success is not controllable. Furthermore, career "promotions" are mostly lateral moves with no increase in pay. 

If there is one positive thing I can take away, it's that I've become skilled at handling nonsense while developing a strong work ethic to survive on little pay. Going forward I know that I will succeed in  any job I pick up in the future exactly because of the many struggles I've endured while at Yelp.

Yelp has an extensive training program that prepares its Account Executives for their role. The training continues from your manager and director throughout your career. The skills you learn during your time at Yelp prepare you for whatever it is that you decide to do in the future. Those that stay at Yelp and are committed to hard work and improvement can build a career unmatched at other companies at such a quick rate.

I ve been working at Yelp Chicago about 11 months. The first thing you’ll realize is that Chicago office is worst revenue office in company by an enormous  margin. If you’re interested in Yelp, I strongly suggest Arizona #1, NYC #2 and also new DC office. The Chicago office is more of a customer service hub, revenue per rep is really bad. It’s  almost impossible to make a commision check and most territories are in very weak yelp zip codes. When you interview for Chicago they never tell you this. Pro tip, absolutely dont  go to Chicago unless your desperate. Also, they have close to 80 managers now in Chicago  so upward movement is virtually impossible. In terms of leadership, Chicago has the weakest. The Directors have been sent here from other offices reluctantly. Lot of turnover. 
Finally , Yelp experience on resume is worthless, trust me. Im finding none of the skills transferable unless its another call center job ....Uuuggghhh.

review_title: Really great people, but you're just a glorified solicitor
review_text: It's truly amazing meeting some of the people you do. The job itself, makes you feel pointless, looking around at 800 people saying the exact same thing you're trained to say. Lack of creativity, but if you really put your mind to it, you can be good at this job. Also, don't listen to the "territory doesn't matter" stuff, because you can get a territory where the area isn't as progressive and YellowPages or something else is still the number 1 in the area. All the managers and directors parrot the exact same things, so it just get's a little annoying hearing "rapport" and them trying to convince you that we're changing lives by sales.
Great location, great people, great place to begin your career! Managers listen to needs and as an office we are moving to a better work life balance.

Very relaxed fun place to work ,I liked my manager. I feel like the pay want sufficient for my experience. Looking to move into a different type of job. I would recommend this job to someone who is just starting off in sales.

Overall, the stress of this position was not worth it when it came to the reality of promotions. I stuck it out for a few months when I thought it had great potential to move me into a position I would like better, but as I learned more about the positions you can move into from the Account Executive position, I was not interested. They paint a picture that the career paths are so great and that you have so much potential to move from your role to a better one, but I had no desire to move into any of the positions above.

Even though I stopped working sooner than I wanted to due to my ill kid , Yelp Inc was the best job ever. I loved the managers, they welcomed my son when I had him during my maternity leave and they did a presentation.

review_title: Great job if you enjoy sales
review_text: This is a heavy volume sales job. You will be trained for 2 months, but you are on t he phones week one. Managers truly do everything they can to set you up for success, but the days are all the same. Calling a small territory offering ad packages, simple enough. You are not expected to reach specific goals for the company until month 4. Free breakfast and Lunch

review_title: Strategic Sourcing Technology manager is incompetent and horrible company
